item.content:encoded:
Friday was a bad day for the New York Yankees even though they opened their final road series of the regular season with a blowout win (NYY 9, ARI 2). Captain Aaron Judge is less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him more than three months. Judge's status for the rest of the season is up in the air.
"I don't have a timeline on him. I'm not going to predict anything. We'll just obviously treat it and see what transpires," manager Aaron Boone said (via MLB.com). "... The reality is, we've had to play a lot of the season this year without him. There's no replacing a player who is as great as Aaron Judge, but we have high expectations. Those don't change now."
The Yankees are always cagey about Judge's injuries. They declined to reveal the severity of the calf strain or give a timetable for his return. Generally speaking, Grade 1 calf strains (the least severe) require 2-3 weeks on the injured list, though calves are very tricky and easy to reinjury. They must be allowed to heal fully, otherwise you risk a more severe injury.
For all intents and purposes, the Yankees are locked into the top wild-card spot. They're six games up in the loss column on the Boston Red Sox, who currently sit in the second wild card spot, plus the Yankees won the season series and have the tiebreaker, so it's really a seven-game lead. New York can clinch the top wild-card spot as soon as Sunday.
The AL East title remains mathematically possible, but it is a long shot. The Yankees are four games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the loss column with four head-to-head games remaining next week in the Bronx. The Rays only need to win one of those four games to clinch the season series and secure the tiebreaker, upping the difficulty for New York.
Just to lay it all out, here's what needs to happen for the Yankees to win the AL East, assuming they sweep those four games against the Rays and clinch the tiebreaker for themselves, which is a pretty big assumption:
- Rays go 6-3 or better: Rays win AL East
- Rays go 5-4: Yankees must go 9-0
- Rays go 4-5: Yankees must go 8-1
- Rays go 3-6: Yankees must go 7-2
- Rays go 2-7: Yankees must go 6-3
- Rays go 1-8: Yankees must go 5-4
- Rays go 0-9: Yankees must go 4-5
The Yankees have already clinched a postseason spot and winning the AL East was a long shot even with Judge. These last nine regular-season games are almost meaningless. If the AL East race gets interesting in a few days, the Yankees can shift gears, but the big picture takes priority this next week. Resting key relievers, lining up the rotation for the Wild Card Series, etc.
"Missing Judge, it hurts. We all know he's the best hitter in the game," Cody Bellinger said (via MLB.com). "For us in here, our mindset is, we're going to have to find a way. I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself. I'm fully confident that we have enough talent in here that we can go out and win, and beat anybody."
With the postseason less than two weeks away, Judge's calf injury creates a lot of questions for both him and the Yankees overall. Here are three questions for the man himself, and his team.
Three questions for Judge
1. Will he return for the postseason? This is really the only question, right? The Yankees are built around Judge being the best hitter in the world, and when he's not, the walls begin to cave in. New York had one of the lowest-scoring offenses in baseball when Judge was out with his rib injury. To paraphrase another New York baseball legend, Judge is the straw that stirs the drink.
Judge is eligible to come off the injured list next Sunday, the final day of the regular season. Roster-wise, he can return in time for the postseason. Health-wise, we have no idea. Calf strains are rarely 10-day absences, but that's what the Yankees have to hope is the case here. There's a very real chance the Yankees are without Judge for at least the Wild Card Series, and maybe longer.
“I’d like to be back by the postseason,” Aaron Judge said. “That’s definitely the plan.”
Said the calf strain involves the soleus muscle — which he said is more crucial to running and hitting — making it more difficult to play through.
2. Will he be himself at the plate? Judge did not go on a minor-league rehab assignment before returning from the rib injury and it showed. He went 4 for 23 (.174) with one walk and 13 strikeouts in his seven games back before the calf injury. His timing was not there at all. Judge's one homer came on a hanging breaking ball. Otherwise, pitchers threw fastballs by him consistently.
To put a number on it, Judge missed with 41% of his swings against fastballs in his seven games back, more than double the 19% league average. This is what it looks like when you miss with more than two out of every five swings against heaters:
It is not exactly a surprise a hitter who did not go on a rehab assignment after spending more than three months on the shelf looked out of sorts at the plate. Judge and the Yankees knew it would take him some time to get back up to speed at the plate, and they were willing to live with it. The goal was always to be ready for the postseason, not so much the regular season.
These last nine games aren't particularly important for the Yankees in the standings, but they were incredibly important to Judge. He needed at-bats to rediscover his timing at the plate, and get back to being the dominant hitter he's been throughout his career. The calf strain puts that on pause. Judge now has even fewer at-bats available to get back to being himself.
3. Will he be able to play the field? There is a scenario in which Judge plays through the calf strain as a full-time DH who doesn't run at 100% (or close to it). How the Yankees would align their defense in that scenario, I have no idea. Ben Rice is a full-time DH these days and also New York's best non-Judge hitter. Platoon-mates Luis Gárcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt are first basemen.
Unless the Yankees do something unexpected, like put Gárcia back at second base (where he was terrible defensively) or Rice back behind the plate (where he was also terrible defensively), slotting Judge in at DH means one of the team's most productive hitters will have to sit. This is something the Yankees will worry about when the time comes, and not a second sooner.
Three questions for the Yankees
1. Where will the righty pop come from? The Yankees have a very lefty-heavy lineup and Judge's righty heft provides important balance. Only the Cleveland Guardians have gotten fewer plate appearances from righties this season. Friday's lineup against Arizona Diamondbacks lefty Eduardo Rodriguez could be what the Yankees run out there against lefties in October:
- 1B Paul Goldschmidt, RHB
- LF Cody Bellinger, LHB
- RF Heliot Ramos, RHB
- DH Ben Rice, LHB
- 3B Amed Rosario, RHB
- CF Spencer Jones, LHB
- SS George Lombard Jr., RHB
- C Austin Wells, LHB
- 2B Anthony Volpe, RHB
Goldschmidt and Ramos are lefty mashers. Bellinger and Rice are very productive left-on-left hitters. Jones has performed well against lefties as a big leaguer, though his minor-league track record against southpaws isn't great. Rosario is having his worst season against lefties. The 7-8-9 spots are unlikely to make an impact offensively, regardless of the pitcher's handedness.
That lineup would look much more imposing with Judge in the No. 3 spot. Perhaps this is not such a big concern though? Since trade deadline day, the Yankees have the highest batting average (.289) and on-base percentage (.362) against lefties, and the third-highest slugging percentage (.456) despite Judge not playing much, and not being much of a factor when he did play.
In all likelihood the Yankees will host the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, and Boston has three quality lefty starters (Jake Bennett, Ranger Suárez, Payton Tolle) and a shutdown lefty relief tandem (Aroldis Chapman, Erik Miller). To beat the Red Sox, the Yankees will need their righty hitters to produce, and now the status of their best right-handed hitter is in question.
2. Will the pitching hold up? Despite not having Judge for more than three months, the Yankees have the American League's best run differential (+143) and second-best record (89-64). They can thank their pitching staff. New York has allowed only 3.68 runs per game this year, the fewest in baseball. Since trade deadline day, it's an incredible 3.37 runs allowed per game.
There are some cracks beginning to form, however. Gerrit Cole has surrendered eight home runs in his last three starts, including five on a four-seam fastball that is no longer the dominant pitch it was at his peak. Max Fried's velocity has been down a tick since returning from a bone bruise in his elbow late last month. That injury has sent him to the injured list twice this year.
Cam Schlittler, the AL Cy Young favorite, has thrown a career-high 184 ⅔ innings with two regular-season starts remaining, plus the postseason. Key late-inning relievers Paul Blackburn, David Bednar, and Brent Headrick have worked a lot -- A LOT -- this season and have all shown a slight dip in velocity in recent weeks, which perhaps is a sign the workload is catching up to them.
Without Judge (and sometimes even with him), the Yankees are a run prevention team. Their superpower is a suffocating pitching staff that is among the best in baseball at limiting hard contact, particularly in the air. With Judge absent, the pitching staff and the ability to prevent runs in general will be of paramount importance. No Judge reduces the margin of error considerably.
3. What about their other injured players? Judge is not the only injured Yankee. Center field Trent Grisham has not played since Sept. 4 due to a Grade 2 hamstring strain. On Friday, Boone said Grisham is pretty far into his running program, and he could make it back before the end of the regular season. That would give the outfield a lift should Judge miss extended time.
Second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. has not played since jamming his thumb sliding into second base on Sept. 8. Boone said Chisholm will come off the injured list when the Yankees return home next week. He's had a down year overall, but Chisholm was playing his best baseball of the season right before the injury. He's an important presence given his speed and defense in particular.
Left-hander Ryan Weathers is working his way back from a flexor strain. He last pitched Aug. 22. Weathers is throwing bullpen sessions, though Boone confirmed he won't return during the regular season. If/when Weathers does return, it will be as a reliever. He has bullpen experience and the Yankees could use middle relief help, but Weathers has to make it back first.
At minimum, Chisholm and Grisham would give the Yankees more options for their Judge-less lineup, even if they only platoon. It wouldn't be hard to find a role for Weathers, who had allowed no more than one run in six of his last seven starts before the injury. Bottom line though, the Yankees need Judge. Everything else is secondary to his return and effectiveness.

Yankees news: Gerrit Cole makes history in win vs. Diamondbacks appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
New York Yankees starter Gerrit Cole made MLB history in Friday night's 9-2 win against the Arizona Diamondbacks at Chase Field.
The 36-year-old earned his 162nd career victory, moving past Mike Moore's 161 wins for the most ever by a pitcher who was selected No. 1 overall in the MLB Draft. Cole was chosen first by the Pittsburgh Pirates in 2011, while Moore went to the Seattle Mariners with the top selection in 1981. David Price is next on the list, ranking third with 157 career wins.
The milestone came as Cole bounced back after allowing seven home runs across his previous two starts, the highest two-game figure of his career. He also had surrendered leadoff home runs in each of those outings.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
After working on his delivery and potential pitch-tipping issues since his previous start against the New York Mets, Cole retired Arizona in order during a 12-pitch opening inning. Corbin Carroll later hit a two-run homer on a four-seam fastball that missed its location, but Cole gave up nothing else to the Diamondbacks.
The right-hander completed six innings, allowing two runs and four hits while issuing no walks and striking out six. He threw 90 pitches, with 62 going for strikes, finishing with a 9-9 record.
New York provided Cole with plenty of early support, sending its first five hitters to base against Eduardo Rodriguez during a five-run opening inning. Ben Rice drew a bases-loaded walk, Amed Rosario delivered an RBI single and George Lombard Jr. added a two-run single.
Rice later launched his 39th homer of the season in the third inning, while Lombard hit his own solo shot in the sixth and finished with three RBIs.
The Yankees improved to 89-64 and moved within four games of the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East with nine games remaining. New York had already secured a postseason berth and has now won 11 of its last 15 games.
Manager Aaron Boone also confirmed that Cole should receive a start if the Yankees reach the American League Wild Card Series.

El novato se lo tomó muy a pecho. El viernes, George Lombard Jr. respondió de la única forma en que puede hacerlo un jugador joven: con un bate lo suficientemente contundente como para ahogar ese recuerdo.
Conectó un sencillo de dos carreras en la primera entrada. Se llevó un jonrón en la sexta. Al final de la noche, sumaba dos hits y tres carreras impulsadas, y el campocorto que parecía desconcertado en Minnesota se mostraba ahora como una pieza clave del equipo.
La coincidencia fue casi cruel por su simetría. La misma tarde en que el equipo se preparaba para recibir el golpe más duro por una lesión en meses, su jugador titular menos consolidado cuajó su partido más sólido.
Lo que podría haber sido un golpe bajo se convirtió en toda una declaración de intenciones. Y esa declaración no tuvo casi nada que ver con el hombre por el que todos estaban preocupados.
Los Yankees arrollaron a los Diamondbacks por 9-2 en el Chase Field el viernes por la noche, unas horas después de enterarse de que Aaron Judge volvería a la lista de lesionados por una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha que podría poner fin a su temporada regular. Nueva York mejoró su balance a 89-64, sumó su undécima victoria en 15 partidos y se colocó a cuatro partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, después de que los Rays perdieran 4-2 ante Boston. Los Yankees también mantuvieron una ventaja de 5 partidos y medio sobre los Red Sox por el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
Una primera entrada de cinco carreras en la que no hizo falta ninguna superestrella
El modelo a seguir para una vida sin Judge quedó claro enseguida. Los Yankees enviaron a 10 bateadores al plato contra el zurdo de Arizona, Eduardo Rodríguez, y anotaron cinco veces antes de que se produjera el segundo out.
Los cinco primeros bateadores llegaron a base. Paul Goldschmidt consiguió una base por bolas , Cody Bellinger conectó un sencillo y, tras otra base por bolas, Ben Rice consiguió una base por bolas con las bases llenas, lo que permitió anotar una carrera. Amed Rosario conectó un sencillo de un toque que impulsó una carrera, un pase fallido permitió que Heliot Ramos anotara y Lombard conectó un sencillo de dos carreras por el centro para poner el 5-0 en el marcador.
No fue un solo golpe fulminante. Fueron nueve bateadores que obligaron a un ex All-Star a lanzar 45 veces en la primera entrada. Esa paciencia es el tipo de ataque que más necesitarán los Yankees en octubre, cuando la ausencia de Judge convierta cada remontada en un esfuerzo colectivo.
Cole se recompone y luego hace historia
La ventaja le permitió a Gerrit Cole respirar tranquilo. El lanzador diestro había encajado siete jonrones en sus dos últimas salidas, y se habían intensificado los rumores sobre si estaría listo para octubre. Con esta actuación, acalló gran parte de esos rumores.
Cole encajó un jonrón de dos carreras de Corbin Carroll en la segunda entrada, de nuevo con una bola rápida que se quedó en el plato, pero nada más. Lanzó seis entradas, cedió dos carreras con cuatro hits, no concedió ninguna base por bolas y ponchó a seis con 90 lanzamientos. Boone había dicho antes del partido que Cole sería el abridor en la serie de comodín de todas formas.
Cole se tomó esta salida como un paso adelante, no como una solución definitiva. Explicó que había dedicado el tiempo entre sus salidas a afinar su lanzamiento para mejorar su capacidad de engaño.
«No creo que lo hayamos hecho perfecto esta noche, pero sí que hemos dado un paso en la dirección correcta», dijo Cole. «Creo que todavía nos queda mucho por hacer. No es fácil, pero es necesario. Así son las grandes ligas».
Esta victoria fue la número 162 de la carrera de Cole, lo que le permitió superar a Mike Moore como el lanzador con más victorias de todos los tiempos entre los elegidos en primera posición en el draft de la MLB, un hito discreto en una noche llena de otros titulares.
Un error defensivo que se corrigió al instante
Esta es la jugada que da forma a la noche, y en la que pocos se fijarán. El error de Lombard dos días antes en Minnesota había formado parte de una secuencia decisiva que le costó a los Yankees un partido que podían haber ganado. El viernes se presentó algo que el deporte rara vez concede tan rápido: una segunda oportunidad sin condiciones.
Su jonrón en la sexta entrada sacó a Rodríguez del partido y amplió la ventaja a 7-2. Para un novato que se vio obligado a ocupar el puesto de campocorto en la recta final, su reacción importó más que las carreras. Cuando le preguntaron por la noche, Lombard lo dejó claro.
«Fue genial desde el principio, todos hicimos buenos turnos al bate», dijo Lombard. «Obviamente, había un buen lanzador en el montículo. Le hicimos trabajar».
Esta actuación llega justo cuando los Yankees están valorando los roles para la postemporada en el cuadro, donde la solidez de un novato ahora tiene un peso real de cara a octubre.
Rice se acerca a los 40 mientras Judge se queda en el banquillo
Rice le dio a los Yankees otro pilar. Su jonrón en la tercera entrada contra Rodríguez recorrió 390 pies y fue el número 39 de la temporada, una cifra que, según el entrenador Aaron Boone, ya había predicho en los entrenamientos de primavera. Rice terminó con ese jonrón y un triple, y suma cinco jonrones en sus últimos 22 partidos.
El ambiente en torno a ese swing era sombrío. Judge había impulsado tantas primeras entradas a lo largo de los años, y ahora los Yankees tienen que volver a luchar por llegar a octubre sin él. Rice se refirió a lo difícil que resulta este momento.
«Es un duro golpe para nosotros», dijo Rice. «Llevábamos mucho tiempo echándole de menos, así que esto nos cuesta especialmente aceptarlo. Pero no nos queda más remedio que seguir jugando a tope y seguir haciendo lo nuestro».
Los Yankees creen que el pitcheo les llevará a la victoria pase lo que pase. Cam Schlittler, el probable ganador del Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, está previsto que sea el abridor en un posible primer partido de la ronda de comodines, con Max Fried y Carlos Rodón como relevos.
Nueva York y Arizona vuelven a enfrentarse este sábado, con Schlittler listo para medirse a Brandon Pfaadt. La inminente serie de cuatro partidos contra los Rays en el Yankee Stadium, que empieza el martes con una doble jornada, podría decidir el título de la división. Por una noche, un novato algo desconcertado y un as que se mantuvo firme hicieron que los Yankees parecieran listos.

PHOENIX - Gerrit Cole nunca había permitido siete jonrones en un lapso de dos aperturas antes de sus salidas más recientes y, con los playoffs a la vuelta de la esquina, existía la preocupación de que el lanzador derecho de los Yankees hubiera sufrido un bajón de rendimiento.
La mayor parte de esa inquietud provenía de fuera del vestuario. El manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone, afirmó el viernes que se esperaba que Cole abriera un partido si su equipo llegaba a la Serie de Comodines de la Liga Americana, y el veterano cumplió su promesa de solucionar el problema de los cuadrangulares y lanzó bien en la victoria por 9-2 sobre los Diamondbacks en el Chase Field el viernes por la noche.
Los Yankees (89-64) ganaron por 11ma vez en 15 partidos, colocándose a cuatro juegos de los Rays en la División Este de la Liga Americana después de que Tampa Bay perdiera ante Boston más temprano esa misma noche.
Horas después de que Cody Bellinger dijera que los Yankees tendrían que "apoyarse mutuamente" para superar la ausencia de Aaron Judge —quien, tras ganar tres veces el premio al Jugador Más Valioso de la Liga Americana, podría perderse el resto de la temporada regular debido a una distensión en la pantorrilla derecha—, los "Bombarderos" respaldaron a Cole con una primera entrada de cinco carreras.
Cada uno de los primeros cinco bateadores se embasó y anotó ante el venzolano Eduardo Rodríguez. Ben Rice negoció una base por bolas con las bases llenas, el dominicano Amed Rosario conectó un sencillo productor y George Lombard Jr. disparó un sencillo de dos carreras; esto fue parte de una noche de tres carreras impulsadas para el novato, quien también conectó un jonrón en la sexta entrada que provocó la salida de Rodríguez del juego.
Rice también conectó su 39no jonrón —líder del equipo— para apoyar a Cole, quien había permitido jonrones al primer bateador en sus dos aperturas anteriores. Tras dedicar tiempo a ajustar su mecánica de lanzamiento y corregir posibles problemas de revelación de pitcheos desde su última salida contra los Mets, Cole retiró a los bateadores de Arizona en orden durante una primera entrada de 12 lanzamientos.
Corbin Carroll conectó un jonrón de dos carreras ante Cole en la segunda entrada, pero eso fue todo lo que lograron los D-backs. Con un total de 90 lanzamientos (62 strikes), Cole permitió cuatro imparables, no otorgó bases por bolas y ponchó a seis bateadores.

item.content:encoded:
The two starting pitchers entered this game trending in opposite directions. Gerrit Cole had just allowed the most home runs (seven) in a two-start span in his career, while Eduardo Rodriguez is in the midst of a career year with a 2.62 ERA. One of those trends remained — Cole giving up another home run on a fastball — but fortunately the other trend was momentarily halted, the Yankees scoring five in the first off E-Rod to give themselves enough of a cushion to weather Cole’s continued home run woes.
Cole settled down after the Carroll dinger to give the Yankees six innings, by which time the offense all but put this game out of reach. They kept the pressure on, scoring a further four runs including solo home runs by Ben Rice and George Lombard Jr., to cruise to a series-opening victory in the desert, 9-2.
Rodriguez came into this game with an ERA above six in the first inning and an ERA right around two for the subsequent innings combined. That made it imperative that the Yankees find a way to do damage before the home team had a chance to come to bat, especially with the rate Cole is giving up the long ball. They did just that with a clear disciplined approach not to expand the zone against E-Rod’s curveball.
Paul Goldschmidt drew a leadoff walk, Cody Bellinger followed with a single, and Heliot Ramos also walked to load the bases with no outs. Rice drew the Yankees’ third walk in the first four batters to plate Goldschmidt and open the scoring, Goldy, Ramos, and Rice all working full counts before taking the free pass. Amed Rosario then fought off a cutter that handcuffed him up and in, muscling it to the opposite field perfectly between center and left fielder to plate Bellinger as the runners went station to station. A wild pitch allowed Ramos to score and Rice and Rosario to move up to second and third. This set up a two-run ground ball single from Lombard that just got by Geraldo Perdomo’s diving attempt to atone for his defensive misplay in the 13th that allowed the Twins to walk off the Yankees on Wednesday.
Rodriguez struck out Volpe to end the inning giving him three strikeouts in the frame, but the damage was done. The 45 pitches he threw were the most he’s thrown in the first inning in his career. 33 of those pitches fell out of the zone, but only eight induced a chase.
It’s a good thing they hung such a crooked number, because Cole immediately gave two of those runs back. He gave up a leadoff single to Perdomo before yanking an 0-1 four-seamer right into Corbin Carroll’s nitro zone, the three-time All-Star obliterating it to right for a two-run bomb to reduce the Yankees’ lead, 5-2. Rice made sure to immediately tilt the momentum back in his team’s favor. After falling behind 0-2, he stayed back on an elevated heater from E-Rod riding it out the other way and over the fence in left-center for a leadoff bomb, his 39th of the year, to give Cole some more of his cushion back, 6-2.
Cole settled down to work a scoreless third and fourth, helped in part by a sharp uptick in slider usage at the expense of some four-seamers as well as an impressive sliding catch in left-center by Spencer Jones in the third. He finally began dialing the fastball command to the corners in the fifth, striking out Tim Tawa and Lars Nootbaar on four-seamers to end the frame after Jesús Sánchez singled with one out. This allowed Lombard to restore the Yankees’ five run lead in the sixth, the rookie punishing a hanging curveball from E-Rod by lining the solo shot down the line it left and into the bullpen for his fourth of the year and third RBI on the night.
The four-seamer was the prime culprit for Cole in his previous two starts with a 68.2-percent hard-hit rate and just six whiffs, and that remained the case tonight. However, I believe it is Cole’s rustiness with his secondaries that is leading his four-seamer to get barreled. The fastball still has plenty of velocity — at 97 mph it’s a full tick above last season. I will grant that he has missed location in the zone on numerous occasions which hasn’t done him any favors.
However, after his last start, Cole identified a lack of chase and whiff against his secondaries as the reason his fastball is getting crushed. Hitters being able to lay off those chase pitches forces Cole to overuse the fastball in counts that favor the softer stuff, which in essence gives them the opportunity to hunt the heater when they should be defending against the breaker. When you can hunt a fastball in any count, chances are you are going to do damage when Cole misses his spot in the zone, the high velocity not much of a weapon when hitters’ bats are preemptively sped up.
Indeed, once he started commanding his slider and knuckle curve to the shadow of the zone in the middle innings, the hard contact against the fastball dried up. Having pitched a strong fifth and sixth and with his pitch count at 90, Boone saw no reason to overextend Cole and ended his night after six with his best innings freshest in mind. He finished night having pitched six innings, allowing two runs on four hits with no walks and six strikeouts.
Despite possessing one of the stingiest bullpens in baseball, the Diamondbacks decided that a five-run deficit in the seventh was too steep to justify using their high leverage arms. So, Zac Gallen made his first career relief appearance, the former All-Star in the midst of am injury-plagued, below-replacement-level campaign. He allowed a leadoff single to Goldschmidt and walked Ramos and Rice — again, both in full counts — to load the bases with one out. Aaron Boone sent out Ryan McMahon to pinch-hit for Rosario, and he hit a sharp grounder to first that Pavin Smith gloved but airmailed the underhand toss to Gallen covering first as all the runners were safe and a run scored on the error. Spencer Jones then appeared to ground into the inning-ending double play, but his hustle out of the box and down the line just beat the throw to pick up an RBI and make it 9-2.
Ryan Yarbrough pitched 1.1 innings in relief of Cole and worked himself into and out of trouble in the seventh. Arizona put runners on second and third as Nolan Arenado singled and Carroll doubled with one out. However, Yarbrough struck out Jose Fernandez and Tawa to strand the pair in scoring position. Rice smoked his fourth triple of the year in the ninth but was stranded at third by a McMahon strikeout. Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil recorded the final five outs of the game without allowing a baserunner to seal the win, 9-2. With the Rays having lost to the Red Sox earlier in the evening, the Yankees’ deficit is back to four games in the division, making that looming four-game set against Tampa in the Bronx even more high stakes.
Cam Schlittler looks to cement his AL Cy Young case tomorrow after Dylan Cease suffered his shortest start of the season on Friday. The Yankees ace will face off against Brandon Pfaadt with a slightly more reasonable game start time. First pitch is scheduled for 8:10 pm ET with the broadcast remaining on YES.
Yankees rout the D-Backs, 9-2, who's your Player of the Game?
Gerrit Cole pitched 6 innings of 2-run ball. George Lombard Jr. hit a two-run single and a solo homer. Ben Rice raked with a solo homer, triple, and two walks.

PHOENIX -- Gerrit Cole had never surrendered seven home runs over a two-start span before his most recent outings, and with the playoffs around the corner, there was concern that the Yankees’ right-hander might have hit a wall.
Most of that came from outside the clubhouse. Yankees manager Aaron Boone affirmed Friday that Cole should expect to draw a start if his team lands in the American League Wild Card Series, and the veteran made good on his promise to fix the long-ball issue, pitching well in a 9-2 victory over the Diamondbacks at Chase Field on Friday night.
Hours after Cody Bellinger said the Yankees would have to “lean on each other” to overcome Aaron Judge’s absence, with the three-time AL MVP potentially set to miss the rest of the regular season with a right calf strain, the Bombers supported Cole with a five-run first inning.
Each of the first five batters reached base and scored against Eduardo Rodriguez. Ben Rice worked a bases-loaded walk, Amed Rosario lifted a run-scoring single and George Lombard Jr. stroked a two-run single -- part of a three-RBI night for the rookie, who launched a sixth-inning homer that chased Rodriguez.
Rice also slugged his team-leading 39th home run to support Cole, who had served up leadoff homers in his previous two starts. Having spent time focusing on his delivery and potential pitch-tipping issues since his last outing against the Mets, Cole set Arizona down in order during a 12-pitch first inning.
Corbin Carroll cracked a two-run homer in the second inning off Cole, but that was all the D-backs managed. Throwing 90 pitches (62 for strikes), Cole scattered four hits, walking none and striking out six.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees open a series in Arizona on Friday night looking to rebound from a one-run loss and find more consistent production from a young outfielder who has shown both power and growing pains.
After falling 5-4 to the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday, the club posted its lineup for the first game against the Diamondbacks, and the most notable tweak involved Spencer Jones, via FantasyPros.
Jones had occupied the fifth spot in the order against Minnesota and finished without a hit while striking out five times. That performance prompted manager Aaron Boone to slide the 25-year-old down one place, into the sixth hole, for Friday’s contest.
The rest of the order features Paul Goldschmidt at first, Cody Bellinger in left, Heliot Ramos in right, Ben Rice as the designated hitter, Amed Rosario at third, George Lombard at short, Austin Wells behind the plate and Anthony Volpe at second. Jones will patrol center field.
The adjustment is modest on paper, yet it reflects the reality of a rookie season that has mixed encouraging numbers with stretches of swing-and-miss. Jones is hitting .252 with 59 hits, 10 home runs, 37 RBIs, 32 runs and nine stolen bases across 79 games.
Those totals represent real production for a player who made his major-league debut earlier this year after being selected in the first round of the 2022 draft out of Vanderbilt.
At 6-foot-7, 240 pounds, he possesses the kind of raw power that can change a game in a single swing, something he demonstrated with a three-run homer against the Twins just a few days earlier.
Still, five strikeouts in one night is the kind of night that forces a lineup shuffle. Boone has moved Jones around the order several times this season as the Yankees try to maximize his strengths while limiting damage against certain pitching looks.
The Diamondbacks series offers another chance to see whether a slightly lower spot in the batting order helps him settle in and put the ball in play more often.
New York arrives in Phoenix needing wins as the calendar moves deeper into September. A tight loss in Minnesota left little margin, and every at-bat from a developing bat like Jones carries extra weight.
The organization drafted him for his combination of size, athleticism and power; the challenge now is translating that package into more consistent contact at the highest level.
Friday’s lineup is a small tactical step in that process rather than a dramatic demotion.
Whether Jones responds with extra-base hits or continues to chase pitches remains to be seen. What is clear is that the Yankees still view him as part of their present and future outfield mix.
A drop from fifth to sixth is not a verdict on his season. It is simply the latest attempt to put a young player in a position where his next good swing can matter.

Ninguno de esos cuatro nunca ha jugado en la postemporada, ya sea con los Yankees o, como es el caso de García y Ramos, con sus equipos anteriores.
Ahora, es posible que algunos de los jugadores veteranos lesionados -- Grisham y Chisholm, específicamente -- puedan regresar a la alineación y enviar a algunos de esos nuevos rostros a la banca o fuera del roster de postemporada por completo. Pero es seguro decir que los Yankees van a contar con al menos algunos novatos en los playoffs el próximo mes, en su búsqueda de ganar su primera Serie Mundial desde el 2009.
Boone ha expresado que sus jóvenes y los recién llegados a los playoffs tienen otra ventaja sobre los jugadores en otros mercados.
"Jugar para los Yankees, jugar en Nueva York”, dijo, "tiene una manera de prepararte para la postemporada”.
Éste ha sido un año de transición en las Grandes Ligas. Consulta la primera ronda del Draft del 2023 si quieres pruebas. No menos de 19 de las 37 selecciones de primera ronda y de compensación han debutado en las Mayores, y muchos de ellos ya son jugadores clave en sus equipos.
"Los jugadores están llegando a las Grandes Ligas a un ritmo muy rápido ahora y a temprana edad”, manifestó el piloto de los Tigers, A.J. Hinch, quien ha dado la bienvenida a la tercera selección Max Clark y al favorito para Novato del Año de la Liga Americana, Kevin McGonigle, a Detroit este año. "No creo que se sientan tan impresionados por los grandes pasos que están dando”.
Para los Yankees, ese grupo incluye a Lombard, quien se ha aclimatado bien desde que fue subido a principios de agosto. Y Jones fue elogiado recientemente nada menos que por Aaron Judge, quien dijo que el jardinero novato "realmente ha evolucionado cada vez que ha sido subido, mejorando un poco más en cada ocasión”.
Por supuesto, habrá contratiempos en el camino. El miércoles, Jones se fue de 6-0 con cinco ponches y cometió un error cuando dejó caer un batazo en el jardín central. Pero cualquiera que siga el béisbol sabe que los días malos y las malas jugadas son parte del ciclo de crecimiento de un jugador de Grandes Ligas. La clave es aprender de ellos para poder limitarlos en el futuro. Y todo ello -- lo bueno, lo malo y lo ocasionalmente feo -- ayuda a preparar a un joven jugador para su primera vez jugando en el béisbol de octubre.
El mundo está a punto de descubrir lo preparados que están los Yankees jóvenes. Pero Jones ofreció un poco de tranquilidad el lunes mientras disfrutaba de la celebración en el vestuario después de la victoria en Target Field que aseguró otra clasificación de Nueva York para los playoffs.
"Creo que para nosotros, jugamos mejor cuando la multitud se vuelve más ruidosa", dijo. "Estoy bien emocionado por lo que está por venir”.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees have a lot of decisions to make for their postseason roster, from lineup construction to the outfield, rotation, and bullpen, to managing guys coming back from injury. Outside of the team's core foundation, almost nothing is settled, especially on the bubble.
One of those bubble spots entails the backup infielders behind a hopefully healthy Jazz Chisholm Jr., George Lombard Jr., and Ryan McMahon. As of right now, the Yankees have three of them on the roster: Jos Caballero, Amed Rosario, and Anthony Volpe. The former has a secured spot due to his speed and versatility, but the latter two aren't as secure.
It's entirely possible the Yankees carry 14 position players on the playoff roster, but that means somebody will have to go for Chisholm when he returns. It's widely believed the corresponding move will be to send Volpe back to the minors, but what if the Yankees went another direction?
Here's why Volpe should be the one who lands that final infield spot instead of Rosario, and how the Yankees can handle the roster math:
New look Anthony Volpe can provide value to Yankees
I am personally not drinking the Kool-Aid of any tangible offensive improvements for Volpe, at least in the short term. What he did at Triple-A was feast on inferior pitchers with his opposite-field approach, something that doesn't have a 1-to-1 conversion rate in the big leagues. That said, we know what he is throughout his career: a mediocre hitter with a career 84 OPS+ and an 89 OPS+ this season in 62 games entering Wednesday.
That said, the ability to hit is maybe the least important aspect for a bench player, particularly one on a team that will have pinch-hitting options on both sides of the plate but needs defenders to replace them.
Volpe was not a fit for this roster when he only played shortstop, something that he would no longer get a chance to do with Lombard entrenched at the position. Upon his demotion to Triple-A, he got experience at second and third base, with the former being the position he's played almost every day since he was recalled after Chisholm's injury. Early returns are positive there.
At this point, we can directly compare Volpe to Rosario, who has also predominantly played second and third base when he has played. While offense is likely not on the 25-year-old's side, defense and baserunning certainly are. He's a vastly superior defender, posting a 3 DRS, 5 FRV, and 5 OAA at shortstop earlier this season.
Volpe is also a much more aggressive baserunner, recording 10 stolen bases and being one of baseball's best at stealing third base, an extremely critical skill to have in close playoff games.
And all of this assumes that Volpe's bat remains as bad as it's been throughout his career. But what if he did make positive adjustments? What if this new approach, coupled with his improved plate discipline from Opening Day, makes him playable, even as a platoon bat? He's already had a few clutch hits, as we saw in the Twins' series.
Amed Rosario's 2026 struggles make him expendable
The one thing that Rosario has on Volpe is his hitting ability, particularly against left-handed pitching, but we've gotten enough samples this season to determine whether a player's reputation actually backs up the results. For Rosario? It's not pretty.
A career .287 hitter against lefties, Rosario is down to just .200 with a .602 OPS against them in 151 plate appearances, something that goes beyond a small sample size. His strikeout rate against them at 21.1 percent is the highest it's been in a decade, while his quality of contact has similarly tanked, even if he's been very unlucky (.262 wOBA vs. .306 xwOBA). Compare this to Volpe, who's slashing a mediocre (but better) .253/.323/.373 against lefties this season, so is Rosario's best strength now a weakness?
He's had pretty hefty reverse splits this season, which completely goes against why he was signed. The Yankees have significantly better options on both sides of the ball against righties, so it doesn't help them at all. When you factor in his defensive shortcomings? He really seems like someone who should be on the chopping block.
Rosario is a guy who can play corner outfield and three infield positions, but plays none of them well. In just 303 innings this season at third base, he has -8 OAA and -7 FRV. He's also managed to be minor negatives in just 48 combined innings in left field, right field, and second base. On a rate basis, he's arguably the worst defender in baseball, something that would be muted if his bat was going (or if the DH spot was more accessible).
He's not a bad baserunner at all. In fact, he's one of the faster guys on the team in terms of sprint speed, but the few times he's on base this season, he's rarely in motion. He has just three stolen bases in the last two seasons and has been a net-negative baserunner according to Baseball Savant's Baserunning Runs metric due to a lack of aggressiveness in taking the extra base.
When your one strength isn't much of a strength anymore, and your usage on the roster is diminished, it has us asking how Volpe could help the team with its roster construction in the postseason.
How the roster shakes out
It wouldn't even be a major roster disruptor. Rosario is almost always the last guy on the bench because of how little the team trusts him defensively. If his bat was that much of an upgrade in a platoon situation, they'd make that trade, but it hasn't.
Come playoff time, I can see a world where the Yankees play Volpe at second or third base in place of McMahon or Chisholm against a left-handed pitcher to increase the at-bat quality without a massive defensive drop-off. It would also give them another pinch-running option they might need in late and close situations, as one of the best base stealers on the team.
I don't expect the Yankees to want to get rid of Rosario, though. He can be left off the playoff roster without a problem. But he can't be removed before then, which could cause an issue if Chisholm is likely to return before the postseason begins.
Therefore, a potential solution could be to send a pitcher down and play with an extra position player down the stretch, but the team is running out of players with options. Volpe could also go down just to fit puzzle pieces and return a few days later.
Ultimately, whatever the Yankees decide, it might not be the difference between a playoff series or even a playoff game, but margins are margins. This has not been a team that has won enough close games late, so giving yourself as much of an advantage in those situations is paramount.

Ryan McMahon's tenure with the New York Yankees hasn't gone as planned. He has certainly been a strong fielder at third base (though not as exceptional as he was sold), but his bat has been anemic by any metric. So much so that after going 0-for-6 with four strikeouts on Wednesday, he has officially joined similar territory as a number of infamous Yankees who underperformed during their time in pinstripes.
As pointed out by Jack Fungo on X, McMahon has a 80 wRC+ in 162 games since being acquired by the Yankees at the 2025 trade deadline. That is a lower mark than DJ LeMahieu's final season with the Yankees when he got released, Josh Donaldson's career in the Bronx, Joey Gallo's time with the Yankees, Isiah Kiner-Falefa's 2023 season and Anthony Volpe's 2025 season.
Ryan McMahon's Yankees company proves the DFA bells are tolling
This isn't great company to be in for McMahon. To put things in perspective, McMahon is 20 points below the league average of 100 for wRC+. On the season, McMahon has hit 10 home runs, has driven in 34 RBI and sports a .210/.275/.346 slash line with a .621 OPS.
McMahon had some solid offensive years with the Colorado Rockies in his career, but his home splits were always much better due to his numbers at Coors Field being inflated as a result of the high altitude. The writing appeared to be on the wall for McMahon before he switched cities.
But the Yankees traded for McMahon because they were desperate for a third baseman last year. They also landed Amed Rosario to platoon with McMahon at the hot corner. Neither has stepped up to claim the job on an everyday basis, though Rosario's bat has been markedly better lately (.348 average in his last seven sporadically placed games).
Should Rosario's hot streak continue into the end of the regular season, the Yankees find a way to utilize him at third base during the postseason. There's even a world where Jose Caballero slides to third, with Anthony Volpe available off the bench. McMahon will probably still get a roster spot, but they cannot play his bat regularly in the biggest games of the year. McMahon's bat creates a black hole in the Yankees' lineup, which they cannot afford to deploy in October.
If not for his defense, McMahon would've likely been designated for assignment by now. And given his historically poor offensive numbers, it seems like it could be headed that way with McMahonunder contract for another year at $16 million. The 31-year-old just has not worked out as a member of the Yankees, and his time in pinstripes should come to an end sooner rather than later.

Baltimore, Maryland.- Paul Goldschmidt conectó un jonrón en el primer lanzamiento del partido, Trent Grisham bateó un cuadrangular de tres carreras y los Yankees de Nueva York vencieron a los Orioles de Baltimore 6-2 el martes por la noche para poner fin a una racha de cuatro derrotas consecutivas.
Will Warren (5-1) permitió dos carreras y cuatro hits en 5 2/3 entradas para los Yankees. Fue una buena actuación para el lanzador derecho, quien había permitido seis carreras en cuatro entradas a Texas en su apertura anterior.
El cuarto jonrón de apertura de Goldschmidt en su carrera y el segundo en cuatro días puso a Nueva York al frente definitivamente, y el batazo de Grisham puso el marcador 6-0 en la tercera entrada. Ambos jonrones fueron contra el zurdo Trevor Rogers, quien solo duró cuatro entradas en su regreso de la lista de lesionados tras una larga enfermedad.
En su primer partido como lanzador desde el 25 de abril, Rogers (2-4) permitió seis carreras y seis hits, elevando su efectividad a 5.77 en comparación con 1.81 en 2025.
Rogers se metió en problemas en la tercera entrada cuando otorgó dos bases por bolas consecutivas que llenaron las bases con un out. Luego, Cody Bellinger bateó un rodado que resultó en un out forzado, produciendo una carrera; Amed Rosario impulsó una carrera con un sencillo al cuadro y Grisham coronó la remontada con su sexto jonrón.
Esa ofensiva fue más que suficiente para asegurar a Nueva York su décima victoria en 11 partidos contra Baltimore, remontándonos a la temporada pasada.
Los equipos lograron superar las cuatro revisiones de decisiones arbitrales que presentaron ante el árbitro principal, Hunter Wendelstedt.
Los Yankees de Nueva York llamaron al campocorto Anthony Volpe de la filial Triple-A de Scranton/Wilkes-Barre y colocaron a José Caballero en la lista de lesionados de 10 días por una fractura en un dedo. Se espera que Volpe sea titular en el último partido de la serie el miércoles.

El partido del miércoles se adelantó a las 13:05 h desde las 18:35 h debido a la amenaza de mal tiempo. Max Fried (4-2, 2.91 ERA) será el abridor por Nueva York, y Kyle Bradish (1-5, 4.83) será el probable abridor por Baltimore.

Will the New York Yankees replace Ryan McMahon at third base this offseason?
The results have not been what Yankees fans were expecting.
Since arriving in the Bronx in July 2025, McMahon is slashing just .211/.290/.346 with 14 home runs and 52 RBI over 522 plate appearances.
This season, he owns a .212/.280/.353 slash line with 10 homers and 34 RBI across 337 trips to the dish, and while McMahon does seem to have an odd knack for getting big hits, his offensive production has been generally unacceptable at the hot corner.
New York was willing to look past that because of his defense, as McMahon posted 10 defensive runs saved and seven outs above average at third base last year. He also regularly posted similar numbers during his time with the Colorado Rockies.
While McMahon has still been wholly solid in the field, a 2026 decline has been evident, as he has posted zero defensive runs saved and three outs above average this season.
Has he been bad at third? Absolutely not. But he has been good enough to justify his $16 million salary while posting a .633 OPS? No.
The problem for the Yankees is that McMahon is under contract for another $16 million next year, which significantly decreases the chances of New York going out and finding an upgrade at the position.
These aren't your dad's Yankees; this is the more financially shrewd, cost-conscious version that initially balked at making any major moves last year due to Marcus Stroman's $18 million salary ... which they eventually ate after releasing him in August 2025.
You can bet that Hal Steinbrenner has every intention of going into 2027 with McMahon as the club's starting third baseman unless Brian Cashman can somehow find a trade for the veteran in which he can offload that money.
McMahon is 31 years old. He'll turn 32 in December. It's entirely possible that the former All-Star is declining, so it's possible that his defensive downturn this season is not a mirage.
Can New York win with McMahon on the roster? Sure. But is it preferable to keep him in a starting role? No.
An alternative solution is fighting a right-handed third baseman who isn't Amed Rosario to man the starting job while keeping McMahon in a reserve role ... but then you are paying $16 million for a pedestrian bench player. That isn't exactly advisable. Especially not for a team that, in recent years, has been trying to cut costs.
And it becomes even less realistic if the MLB does, indeed, institute a salary cap for 2027.
Is it possible the Yankees can trade McMahon? I guess, but good luck finding a team willing to take on the final year of his contract. New York would likely have to absorb some of that $16 million salary, and I'm just not sure how amenable Steinbrenner would be to doing that.
You would think if it meant upgrading the team for just a little bit of extra case, the Yankees would do it. I mean, they're the Yankees, right? But those Evil Empire days appear to be long gone.
The most probable scenario is New York opening up 2027 with McMahon as its starting third baseman, and while it could be worse, it could also be a lot better.
